title: Deuterium From Seawater
lede: Every fusion reaction in the breeder (Hyperion) starts with deuterium, a stable hydrogen isotope present in ordinary seawater.
body: Deuterium is the heavy, stable isotope of hydrogen: one proton, one neutron. It occurs naturally in all water on Earth, mixed with ordinary hydrogen at a fixed ratio set by the planet's water cycle. Because it is already dissolved in the ocean, the breeder (Hyperion) draws its primary fuel from a reservoir that covers most of the planet.

Conventional energy fuels are concentrated deposits that must be located, extracted, and transported from a small number of places. Deuterium is the opposite: it is uniformly distributed in every body of water, so no exploration, mining, or geopolitically constrained supply is involved. Any nation with access to water can obtain the primary fusion fuel.
One deuterium atom accompanies roughly every 6,400 hydrogen atoms in seawater
The isotope is chemically stable and non-radioactive
Standard separation chemistry concentrates it — no exotic process is required
The fuel mass per unit of energy is extremely small

The breeder (Hyperion) is a design and simulation study. Construction begins Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium targeted near 2030. The fuel-supply case described here rests on the natural abundance of deuterium and does not depend on any unproven hardware result. See deuterium abundance and how deuterium is separated.
A fuel that scales with build-out

Because the reservoir is universal, the constraint on fusion energy is never where to find fuel but how many machines are built and operated. That reframes the entire supply conversation: instead of prospecting, refining, and defending access to deposits, a fusion program plans around manufacturing capacity. The fuel is simply present, in the same water everywhere, waiting to be separated by ordinary chemistry.

title: Deuterium Abundance
lede: Deuterium's natural concentration in water is fixed and well measured, which makes the size of the fuel reservoir straightforward to reason about.
body: The deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio in ocean water is a standard reference quantity in geochemistry. On average about 156 deuterium atoms occur for every million hydrogen atoms — close to one part in 6,400 by atom count. This ratio is stable enough that it defines an international water standard used in laboratories worldwide.

From a small fraction to a large reservoir

A small fraction of an enormous reservoir is still an enormous quantity. The world ocean holds a vast mass of water, so even at parts-per-million concentration the total deuterium inventory is measured in scales that dwarf global annual energy demand by many orders of magnitude. The fuel is dilute but effectively unlimited on any human timescale.
The ratio is set by physical chemistry, not by geology or politics
It varies only slightly between oceans and is well characterized
Extraction does not deplete it in any measurable way
The same isotope is present in freshwater, though seawater is the practical source

Because the concentration is known and constant, the breeder (Hyperion) fuel plan does not rely on discovering new deposits. It relies on chemistry that already runs at industrial scale. See longevity of supply and energy density of fusion fuel.

It can seem paradoxical that a fuel present at only parts per million is called inexhaustible. The resolution is scale: the reservoir is so large and the energy per unit of fuel so great that even a tiny concentration yields an astronomical energy content. Dilution is a separation task, not a scarcity, and the separation is routine industrial chemistry rather than exploration or mining.

title: Separating Deuterium
lede: Deuterium is concentrated from water using mature industrial chemistry — no mining, no exotic reagents, and no radioactive input.
body: Because deuterium is chemically almost identical to ordinary hydrogen, it is separated by exploiting small differences in how the two isotopes behave. Two long-established routes dominate: isotopic exchange between water and hydrogen sulfide (the Girdler sulfide process) and water electrolysis, which slightly favors the lighter isotope and enriches the heavier one in the remaining liquid.

These are ordinary chemical-plant operations. The inputs are water and electricity; the outputs are enriched deuterium and depleted water returned to the environment. Nothing in the chain is fissile, and nothing produced is long-lived or radioactive. The environmental burden is dominated by the energy used to run the separation, which is small relative to the energy the fuel later releases in fusion.
Girdler sulfide exchange concentrates deuterium at large scale
Electrolysis performs the final enrichment step
Distillation of hydrogen or water can also be used
No ore, tailings, or extraction waste is generated

The mass of deuterium a fusion plant consumes is minuscule compared with the fuel throughput of combustion or even fission plants. A separation capacity far smaller than existing global heavy-water production would supply a large fleet. See the energy cost of separation and fuel logistics.

Heavy-water production for other purposes has operated at industrial scale for decades, which means the separation know-how, equipment, and safety practice already exist. A fusion fleet would draw on a mature capability rather than inventing one, and because each plant needs so little deuterium, even a modest slice of existing separation capacity could fuel many machines. The front end of the fuel cycle is a solved industrial problem.

title: The Energy Cost Of Separation
lede: Concentrating deuterium takes energy, but that input is a tiny fraction of the energy the fuel later releases in fusion.
body: Any isotope separation costs energy. The relevant question is the ratio between the energy spent enriching the fuel and the energy that fuel then releases. For deuterium the balance is strongly favorable: the fusion energy released per unit mass is enormous, so the separation input is negligible in comparison.

Why the ratio is so lopsided

Fusion draws on the strong nuclear force. The energy released when deuterium fuses is millions of times larger, per atom, than the chemical and electrochemical energies used to separate isotopes. Even generous accounting for the inefficiencies of exchange columns and electrolysis leaves the net energy return dominated overwhelmingly by fusion output.
Separation is an electrochemical and thermal process — modest energy scale
Fusion release is a nuclear process — vastly larger energy scale
The energy payback for the separation step is effectively immediate
Waste heat from separation is ordinary industrial heat, not radioactive

Because the front-end energy is small and can itself be supplied by clean electricity — including, eventually, fusion — the fuel cycle does not carry a hidden energy debt. The breeder (Hyperion) remains a design and simulation study; this energy accounting concerns the fuel supply, not any hardware performance claim. See separation methods.
Payback in the first moments of operation

Because the separation energy is so small next to the fusion yield, the energy invested to prepare a batch of fuel is recovered almost as soon as that fuel begins to react. There is no long energy-debt to amortize, unlike extraction-heavy fuels whose winning and refining can consume a large share of their own output. The fuel cycle carries no hidden energy penalty that would erode its net benefit.

title: Longevity Of Supply
lede: At any plausible rate of global energy use, the deuterium in the ocean represents a fuel supply lasting far beyond human timescales.
body: The size of the deuterium reservoir, combined with the extraordinary energy density of fusion fuel, means the practical limit on supply is not the fuel. The ocean's deuterium inventory could meet global energy demand for a span best measured in millions of years, not decades or centuries. On any planning horizon that matters, the primary fuel is inexhaustible.

Most energy debates are, at bottom, debates about scarcity: where the fuel is, who controls it, and how long it lasts. A fuel that is uniformly distributed and effectively unlimited removes that constraint from the conversation. Planning can focus on building and operating plants rather than on securing and rationing fuel.
The reservoir is not meaningfully depleted by use
No new discovery is required to extend supply
Supply is decoupled from any single region or deposit
Longevity holds even under aggressive growth in global energy demand
This durability is a foundation of the sustainability case. See a sustainable fuel cycle and no fuel-supply geopolitics.

When a fuel outlasts any meaningful planning horizon, scarcity drops out of the strategic picture entirely. Decisions that normally hinge on reserves — where to site plants, how to sequence a fleet, how to hedge against depletion — become simple, because the fuel is not the limiting factor. What remains is engineering and construction, which are problems a program can actually control.

title: Helium-3 Bred In Situ
lede: The breeder (Hyperion) produces helium-3 as part of its own fuel cycle, so the isotope is made on site rather than mined.
body: Helium-3 as a product, not a purchase

Helium-3 is one of the scarcest useful isotopes on Earth. The breeder (Hyperion) generates it in situ: neutrons from deuterium-tritium fusion breed tritium in a lithium blanket, and that tritium decays into helium-3. The isotope emerges as a natural output of running the machine, in a design-target class of about 1.97 kg per year.

Terrestrial helium-3 is present only in trace amounts, and the historical supply has depended on the decay of tritium held in defense stockpiles. That supply is limited and shrinking. A machine that breeds its own helium-3 turns a scarce, contested isotope into a renewable byproduct of energy operations.
Design-target output on the order of 1.97 kg/yr of helium-3 per breeder
The isotope is produced continuously as tritium decays
No lunar mining or atmospheric extraction is required for this route
Also produced: a roughly 4 kg/yr tritium class and 14 MeV neutrons

These are computed design targets for a machine now entering construction (Q2 2027), not measured yields. First-of-a-kind first tritium is targeted near 2030. See no mining required and tritium decay to helium-3.
Turning a scarce isotope into an output

The significance of in-situ breeding is that it inverts helium-3 from something a program must acquire into something a program produces. Every operating breeder becomes a small, continuous source, so the total available supply grows with the fleet rather than being fixed by legacy stockpiles. This is why the isotope is treated as a renewable product of energy operations rather than a commodity to be hunted down.

title: Helium-3 Without Mining
lede: Because helium-3 is bred from lithium and hydrogen isotopes, the breeder needs no terrestrial or lunar mining to obtain it.
body: Historically, helium-3 has come from two hard sources. On Earth it is recovered almost entirely from the radioactive decay of tritium in aging weapons stockpiles — a fixed and declining inventory. The frequently discussed alternative is mining lunar regolith, which would require an entire off-world extraction and transport program. Both routes are constrained.

The breeder route sidesteps both problems. Its feedstocks are deuterium from water and lithium for the breeding blanket — both abundant and already produced industrially. The helium-3 appears as tritium decays, so the plant becomes a continuous, renewable source of an isotope that otherwise demands either weapons material or a lunar mission.
No ore body, tailings, or mine footprint on Earth
No lunar landing, excavation, or return logistics required
Feedstocks (water-derived deuterium, lithium) are common and benign
Supply scales with the number of operating plants, not with mining capacity
This is central to the resource-sustainability case. See helium-3 bred in situ and lithium for the blanket.

Both inputs to the breeding route — water-derived deuterium and blanket lithium — are among the most accessible materials on Earth, and neither requires a dedicated extraction industry built specifically to supply fusion. This is the sharpest contrast with the lunar route, which would need launch, landing, excavation, processing, and return infrastructure before a single gram arrived. Breeding replaces that entire chain with a machine that is already running to make energy.

title: Helium-3 Scarcity In Context
lede: Helium-3 is one of the rarest useful isotopes on Earth; understanding that scarcity explains why breeding it changes the picture.
body: Helium-3 is a light, stable isotope that the Earth does not naturally retain. Primordial helium-3 largely escaped to space, and the small amounts present today come mostly from the decay of tritium. Because tritium itself is rare and short-lived, the terrestrial helium-3 inventory is tiny and difficult to grow.

Helium-3 is prized for uses that have no easy substitute: ultra-low-temperature refrigeration for quantum and superconducting systems, neutron detection for security screening, and medical imaging. Demand for these applications has repeatedly exceeded what the legacy stockpile-decay supply can provide, producing recurring shortages.
Legacy supply depends on decaying weapons tritium — a shrinking source
No large natural deposit exists to be discovered on Earth
Existing uses already compete for a constrained inventory
A renewable source would relieve that constraint

A breeder (Hyperion) that produces helium-3 as an operational byproduct converts a scarce, contested isotope into a renewable one. This reframes helium-3 from a strategic bottleneck into a sustainable output of energy infrastructure. Note that helium-3's strategic value is not an economic claim on this site — it is a statement about physical scarcity and supply. See helium-3 bred in situ.
A bottleneck turned into a byproduct

For decades helium-3 has been a recurring bottleneck: shortages have delayed research programs and forced users to ration a dwindling stock. A renewable source changes the character of the problem from managing scarcity to managing production. The isotope no longer sits at the mercy of an aging inventory; it becomes an ordinary output that scales with how much fusion infrastructure exists.

title: Tritium Breeding Ratio As A Design Lever
lede: The tritium breeding ratio measures how much tritium a machine makes per unit consumed; the breeder studies it across values of 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8.
body: Deuterium-tritium fusion consumes tritium, which is not abundant in nature. A fusion plant must therefore breed its own tritium in a lithium blanket surrounding the plasma. The tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is the number of tritium atoms produced per tritium atom burned. A TBR above one means the plant makes more than it consumes.

Why it is treated as a lever, not a fixed number

The achievable TBR depends on blanket geometry, lithium enrichment, neutron multipliers, and how much of the neutron flux the structure captures. Rather than assert a single value, the breeder (Hyperion) design studies span 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8 to bracket the trade space. Higher ratios build a fuel surplus faster; lower ratios are easier to engineer.
A TBR above one is required for fuel self-sufficiency
Surplus tritium can start additional machines or decay into helium-3
The lever couples to blanket design and neutron economy
Local breeding and net delivered breeding are distinguished carefully

These are design-study values, not demonstrated blanket performance. Reconciling local versus net breeding is an open engineering question the program tracks explicitly. See tritium self-sufficiency and the neutron economy.
Why bracketing beats a single claim

Quoting one breeding ratio would imply a precision the physics does not yet support. By reporting a sweep across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, the design study makes its assumptions visible and lets each downstream conclusion be traced to a stated value. This honesty also foregrounds the key uncertainty — the gap between what is bred locally and what is delivered after losses — rather than hiding it inside a single confident number.

title: Tritium Decays To Helium-3
lede: Tritium is radioactive with a 12.3-year half-life, and its only decay product is stable helium-3 — the physical basis for breeding the isotope.
body: Tritium is the heaviest hydrogen isotope: one proton, two neutrons. It is unstable and undergoes beta decay with a half-life of about 12.3 years, emitting a low-energy electron and turning into helium-3. The helium-3 produced is stable and permanent. This one decay is what links the tritium a breeder makes to the helium-3 it supplies.

Why the low decay energy matters

The beta particle from tritium decay is very low in energy and travels only a short distance in air; it cannot penetrate skin from outside. This makes tritium comparatively benign to handle relative to many radioisotopes, though it is still managed carefully because it can be incorporated into water. The decay produces no gamma radiation.
Half-life about 12.3 years — no long-lived legacy
Sole decay product is stable helium-3
Beta emission only, low energy, no gamma rays
The decay is what lets stored tritium become a helium-3 source

Because the decay is slow and predictable, tritium held in inventory steadily converts into recoverable helium-3. A breeder (Hyperion) with a tritium surplus therefore accumulates helium-3 over time as a natural consequence of physics. See helium-3 bred in situ and recovering the isotope.

This single, well-understood decay is the hinge of the whole Kronos isotope story. It is what lets a machine that runs on tritium become a supplier of helium-3, and it is what guarantees that leftover tritium turns into something useful rather than lingering as a hazard. Few nuclear processes are as clean in their bookkeeping: one unstable atom in, one stable and valuable atom out.

title: Tritium Self-Sufficiency
lede: A deuterium-tritium plant must breed all the tritium it burns; self-sufficiency is what makes the fuel cycle closed and independent of external supply.
body: Tritium does not exist in usable natural quantities, and the world inventory is small. A deuterium-tritium machine that relied on external tritium could not scale. The breeder (Hyperion) is therefore designed to breed at least as much tritium as it consumes, closing the loop so the plant sustains its own fuel with only deuterium and lithium coming in.

Breeding above unity does more than sustain one machine. A surplus can be used to provide the initial tritium charge for the next plant, so a fleet can grow from its own production rather than waiting on scarce external stocks. Surplus tritium not needed for startup decays into recoverable helium-3, feeding the isotope supply.
Inputs to the loop are only deuterium and lithium — both abundant
Breeding ratio above one is the condition for growth
Surplus starts new machines or becomes helium-3
External tritium dependence is designed out of the cycle

Demonstrating true net self-sufficiency in real blankets — accounting for losses, retention, and geometry — is an open engineering problem the program tracks. The breeder is a design and simulation study; first-of-a-kind first tritium is targeted near 2030. See the breeding-ratio lever and the closed fuel cycle.

Abundance of deuterium and lithium is necessary but not sufficient; a plant also needs to close its tritium loop, because tritium cannot simply be bought in quantity. Self-sufficiency is therefore the property that converts abundant raw inputs into genuine fuel independence. A machine that breeds and recovers its own tritium answers to no external fuel supplier at all once it is running.

title: Lithium For The Breeding Blanket
lede: Tritium is bred when blanket lithium absorbs fusion neutrons; lithium is abundant, widely distributed, and used in modest quantities per plant.
body: The breeding blanket that surrounds the plasma contains lithium. When a 14 MeV fusion neutron strikes a lithium nucleus, the reaction produces tritium (plus helium). This is the mechanism that lets a deuterium-tritium plant manufacture its own fuel. Lithium, together with deuterium from water, is one of only two consumable inputs to the closed cycle.

Lithium is a common element found in brines and mineral deposits on every inhabited continent, and it is already produced at large industrial scale. The amount a fusion blanket consumes to breed a year of tritium is small compared with global lithium production, and it is not in direct competition with the far larger tonnages used elsewhere.
Lithium occurs in brines and ores across many regions
Blanket consumption per plant is modest
Both natural lithium isotopes participate in breeding reactions
Lithium can be recovered and recycled within the blanket system

Because lithium is geographically dispersed and the quantities are small, it does not reintroduce the supply concentration that fusion is meant to escape. See lithium-6 versus lithium-7 and lithium recycling in the blanket.

Lithium is the only mined material the fuel cycle depends on, and it enters in small, recyclable quantities from sources spread across many regions. This keeps the cycle from quietly reintroducing the supply concentration that fusion is meant to escape, and it means the blanket does not compete meaningfully with the far larger lithium demands of other industries. The second input is as benign, in supply terms, as the first.

title: Lithium-6 Versus Lithium-7
lede: The two natural lithium isotopes breed tritium by different reactions, and their balance is a design lever for the breeding blanket.
body: Natural lithium is a mix of two stable isotopes: lithium-6 (about 7.5%) and lithium-7 (about 92.5%). Both breed tritium, but differently. Lithium-6 captures a slowed neutron and reliably yields tritium plus helium. Lithium-7 reacts with fast neutrons, producing tritium, helium, and — importantly — an additional neutron, which can help sustain the breeding chain.

The proportion of lithium-6 in the blanket is a design choice. Enriching lithium-6 raises the reliable, high-yield breeding channel, while retaining lithium-7 preserves the neutron-multiplying reaction that feeds the neutron economy. Tuning this balance is one of the levers that sets the achievable tritium breeding ratio.

The isotope balance is set together with the rest of the neutron budget. See the neutron economy and the breeding-ratio lever.

Having two breeding channels in the same element gives designers a genuine lever rather than a fixed constraint. By choosing how much lithium-6 to enrich, a blanket can favor reliable thermal capture or preserve the fast reaction that returns an extra neutron to the budget. The natural isotope mix is only a starting point; the working blanket is tuned deliberately to hit the target breeding ratio.

title: The Deuterium-Tritium Fuel Cycle
lede: The breeder (Hyperion) runs on deuterium and tritium, breeding its own tritium so the cycle closes with only water-derived and abundant inputs.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) fuses deuterium with tritium. This reaction releases a helium nucleus and an energetic 14 MeV neutron. The neutron carries most of the released energy and is also the agent that breeds new tritium in the surrounding lithium blanket, which is what makes the cycle self-sustaining.

The breeder is a spherical tokamak. Its design-point figures include a scientific gain (Q) of 3.424, fusion power of 88.7 MW, plasma current of 9.86 MA, a peak field of 16.84 T (about 8 T on axis), and negative triangularity of -0.30. These are computed design targets, not measurements.

Fuel bred: tritium, in a roughly 4 kg/yr class
Byproduct isotope: helium-3, about 1.97 kg/yr class

Construction begins Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted near 2030; there is no hardware net-gain claim before that milestone. See the burner's deuterium-helium-3 cycle and the closed fuel cycle.
Neutrons that both power and breed

What makes the deuterium-tritium cycle self-sustaining is that its energetic neutron plays two roles at once: it carries most of the released energy and it is the agent that manufactures the next generation of fuel. Capturing that neutron well is therefore both an energy question and a fuel question, which is why blanket design sits at the center of the machine rather than at its periphery.

title: The Deuterium-Helium-3 Fuel Cycle
lede: The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) fuses deuterium with helium-3, a reaction whose main products are charged particles rather than neutrons.
body: The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a tandem-mirror generator that fuses deuterium with helium-3. The primary reaction produces charged particles — a proton and a helium-4 nucleus — rather than a neutron. Charged particles can be converted directly to electricity, and the low neutron output eases materials and shielding demands. A residual neutron fraction of about 5.44% arises from side reactions.

Helium-3 is scarce on Earth, so the burner's fuel depends on a helium-3 source. In the Kronos picture that source is the breeder (Hyperion), which produces helium-3 in situ, complemented over the longer term by lunar helium-3. The two machines are thus linked: the breeder makes fuel the burner can use.
Design plug field 26.49 T; throat field 17 T
Neutron fraction about 5.44% — much lower than deuterium-tritium
Direct energy conversion of charged products, no steam cycle required
Housings: Aegis (fixed defense installations) and MetroVolt (data centers)

The burner is a design and simulation study, and its commercial fuel supply is gated on scaling helium-3 production; nothing here claims demonstrated net power. See the breeder's deuterium-tritium cycle and the Earth-Moon fuel picture.

The appeal of deuterium-helium-3 is that its primary products are charged particles whose energy can be converted to electricity directly, without boiling water to drive a turbine. That both simplifies the plant and sharply reduces the neutron burden on materials. The trade is that helium-3 is scarce, which is precisely the problem the breeder is meant to solve by making the isotope on Earth.

title: No Fuel-Supply Geopolitics
lede: Because the fuel comes from seawater and is bred on site, fusion removes the resource-control dynamics that shape conventional energy.
body: Conventional energy is entangled with geography. Oil, gas, uranium, and the minerals for batteries are concentrated in specific regions, which creates chokepoints, dependencies, and leverage. Much of the world's energy diplomacy exists because the fuel is scarce and unevenly distributed.

What changes when fuel is everywhere

Deuterium is present in all seawater and freshwater, and the helium-3 and tritium a plant needs are bred on site from lithium and water. No importable ore or refined fuel sits at the center of the supply chain. A country can fuel its plants from its own water, which turns energy security into a question of building capacity rather than securing deposits.
Primary fuel is uniformly distributed worldwide
No pipelines, tanker routes, or ore imports are required
No fissile material enters or leaves the fuel cycle
Supply cannot be cut off by controlling a deposit or a strait
Abundance is itself a security property: a fuel that cannot be monopolized cannot be weaponized as leverage. See energy security through abundance and no mining footprint.

Scarcity is what gives a fuel geopolitical weight; a resource that can be withheld can be used as leverage. A fuel drawn from every ocean and bred inside the plant cannot be cornered, embargoed, or monopolized. Removing that leverage does not merely lower cost pressure — it changes the strategic character of energy from a contest over deposits into a question of who chooses to build.

title: Energy Security Through Abundance
lede: When fuel is universally available and bred on site, energy security shifts from controlling supply to building capacity.
body: Traditional energy security means securing access to a scarce resource: diversifying suppliers, stockpiling reserves, and protecting supply routes. Fusion offers a different model. If the fuel is drawn from local water and bred in the plant, security comes from having built the plant, not from access to a distant deposit.

A fuel that every nation can obtain locally is resilient against the disruptions that affect concentrated supplies: embargoes, blockades, price shocks tied to a single region, and the loss of a critical facility. The small mass of fuel involved also means that even modest domestic stockpiles cover long operating periods.
No dependence on foreign fuel producers
Small fuel mass makes strategic reserves easy to hold
Resilience scales with domestic build-out, not with resource access
A complement to firm clean power

This resilience pairs with the operational profile of fusion as clean, firm power that complements variable renewables. Security of supply and reliability of output reinforce each other. See no fuel geopolitics and fuel logistics.
Reserves measured in years, not days

Because the fuel mass is so small, even a modest on-site stockpile represents a very long operating reserve, far beyond the days-to-weeks buffers typical of fuel-hungry plants. A nation can hold a strategic fuel reserve in a space that would be trivial by conventional standards. Resilience thus comes almost for free from the extraordinary energy density of the fuel.

title: Compared To Uranium Mining And Enrichment
lede: The fusion fuel cycle avoids uranium's ore mining, enrichment, and long-lived spent fuel, and it produces no fissile material.
body: A uranium fuel cycle begins with mining ore, milling it into concentrate, converting and enriching it to raise the fissile isotope, and fabricating fuel elements. Each step has an environmental and material footprint, and enrichment produces material that must be safeguarded against diversion.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 148" width="100%" style="max-width:680px;height:auto;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="1" y="1" width="678" height="146" rx="10" fill="#232C39" stroke="#B8933F" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="15" fill="#D4AD5C" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">Fuel-chain burden: uranium vs fusion (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="74" font-size="12" fill="#E8ECF1" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">Uranium: mine + enrich + guard</text><rect x="210" y="62" width="400" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#33404f" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="62" width="400" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="618" y="75" font-size="11" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">extractive + safeguarded</text><text x="24" y="108" font-size="12" fill="#E8ECF1" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">Fusion: separate water + breed</text><rect x="210" y="96" width="400" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#33404f" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="96" width="48" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="618" y="109" font-size="11" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">chemistry + in-plant breeding</text><text x="24" y="140" font-size="10" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">bar length indicates supply-chain burden, not volume</text></svg>

The fusion fuel cycle has no ore body. Deuterium comes from water, and tritium and helium-3 are bred on site from lithium. There is no enrichment of a fissile isotope, so there is no enrichment infrastructure to guard and no weapons-usable fuel stream. The fuel inputs are chemically benign and abundant.
No uranium mine, mill, or tailings pile
No isotopic enrichment of fissile material
No long-lived spent-fuel inventory to store for millennia
No fissile fuel that could be diverted

This page compares fuel cycles, not the full lifecycle of any specific plant, and makes no economic claim. Activation of structural materials by neutrons is addressed separately in the low-neutron and waste pages. See fusion versus fission versus fossil.
A front end without a mine or a guard

The uranium cycle carries two burdens the fusion cycle simply lacks: an extractive front end with ore, mills, and tailings, and a safeguards regime around enrichment and fissile material. The fusion cycle has neither. Its front end is water chemistry, and it never creates a weapons-usable stream, so the apparatus of mining and of nuclear safeguards that surrounds fissile fuel has no counterpart here.

title: Compared To Fossil Fuel Supply Chains
lede: Fossil energy depends on continuous extraction and transport of large fuel masses; fusion runs on a tiny mass of fuel drawn from water.
body: A fossil plant is a fuel-consuming machine on an enormous scale. It requires a constant stream of coal, oil, or gas delivered by mine, pipeline, rail, or tanker, and it emits combustion products continuously. The supply chain — extraction, processing, and transport of large tonnages — is a permanent operating burden.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 182" width="100%" style="max-width:680px;height:auto;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="1" y="1" width="678" height="180" rx="10" fill="#232C39" stroke="#B8933F" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="15" fill="#D4AD5C" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">Fuel mass throughput per unit energy (schematic, log intuition)</text><text x="24" y="74" font-size="12" fill="#E8ECF1" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">Coal</text><rect x="210" y="62" width="400" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#33404f" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="62" width="400" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="618" y="75" font-size="11" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">very large mass</text><text x="24" y="108" font-size="12" fill="#E8ECF1" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">Natural gas</text><rect x="210" y="96" width="400" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#33404f" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="96" width="240" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="618" y="109" font-size="11" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">large mass</text><text x="24" y="142" font-size="12" fill="#E8ECF1" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">Fusion fuel</text><rect x="210" y="130" width="400" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#33404f" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="130" width="4" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="618" y="143" font-size="11" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">grams-scale</text><text x="24" y="174" font-size="10" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">bars indicate order-of-magnitude intuition, not exact ratios</text></svg>

Fusion inverts this. The energy density of the fuel is so high that the mass consumed is minuscule, and the fuel is obtained from water rather than extracted from deposits. There is no continuous stream of combustion products, no ash, and no need for a large, region-dependent extraction industry feeding the plant.
Fuel mass per unit energy is smaller by orders of magnitude
No mines, wells, pipelines, or tankers in the fuel chain
No carbon dioxide or combustion pollutants from the reaction
Fuel is sourced locally from water everywhere
The comparison concerns the fuel supply chain and the fusion reaction itself; it makes no economic claim. See energy density of fusion fuel and the three-way comparison.

A fossil plant is defined by throughput: it must be fed continuously and it emits continuously, so its supply chain is a permanent, heavy-transport operation. Fusion breaks that dependence because the fuel mass is so small and largely bred on site. The difference is not incremental but categorical — a continuous stream of tonnes replaced by an occasional handling of kilograms.

title: Compared To Battery And Rare-Earth Minerals
lede: Fusion's fuel does not draw on the concentrated critical-mineral supply chains that constrain many clean-energy technologies.
body: Many clean-energy technologies depend on specific minerals — lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare-earth elements — whose production is concentrated in a few countries and whose extraction carries real environmental cost. These supply chains introduce their own geopolitics and scaling limits.

The fusion fuel cycle needs water-derived deuterium and lithium for breeding. Lithium is common and widely distributed, and the quantity a blanket consumes is small. The fuel chain does not require cobalt, nickel, or rare-earth elements, so it sits outside the most constrained critical-mineral markets.
No cobalt or nickel in the fuel cycle
No rare-earth elements required to make fuel
Lithium use is modest and geographically dispersed
The fuel itself is not a mined mineral at all

This concerns the fuel supply, not every material in a complete plant, which like any large machine uses structural metals and superconductors. The comparison is physical, not economic. See lithium for breeding and no mining footprint.

Many low-carbon technologies trade one supply constraint for another, leaning on cobalt, nickel, or rare earths whose production is concentrated and contested. The fusion fuel cycle sits outside those markets: it needs no rare earths and no cobalt, only water and common lithium in small amounts. Whatever critical materials a full plant uses in its structure, the fuel itself does not add to that pressure.

title: A Sustainable Fuel Cycle
lede: Sustainability here means a fuel cycle whose inputs are abundant, whose loop is closed, and whose operation does not deplete a scarce resource.
body: Three properties of a sustainable cycle

A fuel cycle can be called sustainable when three conditions hold: its inputs are effectively unlimited, it does not accumulate an unmanageable waste legacy, and it can be run indefinitely without depleting a finite deposit. The fusion fuel cycle is designed to meet all three.

Only two materials enter: deuterium from water and lithium for the blanket. Inside the plant the tritium is bred and recovered, so the fuel regenerates rather than being consumed from an external store. Helium-3 emerges as a useful product. The loop is closed in the sense that the plant does not depend on a continuing external fuel supply once running.
Inputs are abundant and universally available
Tritium is regenerated inside the loop, not imported
No long-lived spent fuel is produced
The cycle can run on any planning horizon that matters

The closed cycle is a design goal for machines that are still simulation studies; demonstrating true net breeding and recovery is open work. Construction begins Q2 2027. See the closed fuel cycle and sustainability metrics.
Sustainability as a set of physical facts

Calling a cycle sustainable is only meaningful if it rests on physical facts rather than aspiration. Here the facts are concrete: the inputs are effectively unlimited, the tritium loop regenerates internally, and the cycle leaves no long-lived fuel waste. Each is a checkable property of the fuel and the reactions, which is why the sustainability claim can be stated plainly and defended.

title: No Mining Footprint For Fuel
lede: Neither the deuterium nor the bred helium-3 requires ore extraction, so the fuel cycle carries no mine, tailings, or excavation footprint.
body: Most energy fuels begin at a mine or well: an excavation with tailings, water use, land disturbance, and a fixed location. This footprint is unavoidable when the fuel is a concentrated deposit that must be dug up and refined.

The fusion fuel chain has no mine

Deuterium is separated from water by chemistry, not dug from the ground. Tritium and helium-3 are bred inside the plant. The only mined input is lithium, which is used in small quantities and can be recycled within the blanket. There is no ore body, no tailings pile, and no excavation dedicated to the fuel itself.
No fuel mine and no associated tailings
No land committed to fuel extraction
Lithium is the sole mined input, used sparingly and recyclable
Helium-3 needs neither terrestrial nor lunar mining on this route
Replacing extraction with chemistry and in-plant breeding removes an entire category of environmental impact from the fuel supply. See helium-3 without mining and lithium recycling.
Removing a whole category of impact

Mining is not one impact but a bundle — land disturbance, tailings, water use, and a fixed location that must be developed and eventually remediated. Sourcing fuel from water and breeding it in the plant removes that entire bundle from the fuel supply at once. What remains, a modest and recyclable lithium demand, is a small fraction of the footprint that conventional fuels impose before a single unit of energy is produced.

title: Energy Density Of Fusion Fuel
lede: Fusion releases millions of times more energy per unit mass than chemical fuels, which is why the required fuel mass is so small.
body: Burning a fuel rearranges electrons and releases chemical-bond energy. Fusing nuclei taps the strong nuclear force and releases far more energy per reaction. Per unit mass of fuel, fusion yields on the order of a million times more energy than combustion. This single fact drives most of the fuel-supply advantages of fusion.

High energy density means a plant consumes very little fuel mass. A tiny extraction rate from an enormous reservoir then supplies a great deal of energy, which is exactly why deuterium can be dilute in seawater yet still constitute an effectively unlimited supply. Density and abundance work together.
Fusion energy per unit mass dwarfs chemical fuels
Small fuel mass makes transport and storage trivial
Dilute fuel is still abundant because so little is needed
The breeder design point releases 88.7 MW of fusion power
The 88.7 MW figure and the breeder's scientific gain of 3.424 are computed design targets, not measured performance. See fuel logistics and deuterium abundance.

Almost every downstream benefit of fusion fuel traces back to its energy density. Small fuel mass follows from it, which makes logistics trivial and reserves easy; tolerance of dilute sources follows from it, which makes seawater a viable reservoir; and the negligible separation-energy penalty follows from it. Understanding the density is understanding why the fuel-supply case looks so different from every combustion or fission comparison.

title: Fuel Logistics
lede: Because the fuel mass is tiny and partly bred on site, moving and storing fusion fuel is a small-scale operation.
body: A fusion plant's annual fuel throughput is measured in kilograms, not the millions of tonnes a fossil plant burns. Deuterium can be produced near the plant from water, and tritium is bred internally. What must be handled externally is small in quantity, which makes fuel logistics a modest activity rather than a continuous heavy-transport operation.

Small quantity does not mean no handling. Tritium is radioactive and mobile, so it is contained, accounted for, and recovered rather than released. Deuterium and helium-3 are stable and benign. The logistics challenge is precision and containment for tritium, not the tonnage that dominates conventional fuel supply.
Annual fuel mass is on the order of kilograms
Deuterium is produced locally from water
Tritium is bred and recovered inside the plant
Helium-3 and deuterium are stable and easy to store
A small fuel mass means even a long operating reserve occupies little space, reinforcing the security-through-abundance argument. See energy security and fuel storage and handling.

The logistics challenge of fusion fuel is not scale but care: the quantities are tiny, so the work shifts from moving mass to containing and accounting for a small, radioactive tritium inventory. That is a fundamentally more tractable problem than a continuous heavy-transport chain. The stable components, deuterium and helium-3, are handled like ordinary industrial gases, adding little burden.

title: The Ocean As A Fuel Reservoir
lede: The world ocean is an enormous, self-renewing store of hydrogen, and the deuterium within it is the practical source of primary fusion fuel.
body: The ocean holds a vast mass of water, and every water molecule contains hydrogen with its fixed fraction of deuterium. Treating the ocean as a fuel reservoir, the total deuterium inventory is staggering — large enough that human energy use would draw on it at an imperceptible rate for millions of years.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 260" width="100%" style="max-width:680px;height:auto;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="1" y="1" width="678" height="258" rx="10" fill="#232C39" stroke="#B8933F" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="15" fill="#D4AD5C" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">The ocean is the practical deuterium reservoir</text><rect x="40" y="70" width="500" height="150" rx="6" fill="#16303c" stroke="#B8933F" stroke-width="1"/><text x="290" y="150" font-size="12" fill="#E8ECF1" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">ocean hydrogen reservoir</text><text x="290" y="170" font-size="10" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(effectively inexhaustible)</text><rect x="556" y="70" width="4" height="150" rx="2" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="568" y="100" font-size="10" fill="#D4AD5C" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">extracted</text><text x="568" y="114" font-size="10" fill="#D4AD5C" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">fraction</text><text x="568" y="132" font-size="10" fill="#9AA6B2" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">extraction is imperceptible</text></svg>

Water is not consumed by extracting deuterium; the depleted water returns to the environment and rejoins the hydrological cycle. The reservoir is effectively self-renewing on human timescales, and the deuterium ratio it maintains is stable. Freshwater carries the same isotope, but the ocean is the largest and most convenient source.
The ocean's deuterium inventory is planetary in scale
Water returns to the environment after separation
The isotope ratio is naturally maintained

The path from ocean to fuel is chemical separation, not extraction of a deposit, which is why the reservoir framing is apt: fusion draws fuel from a distributed store rather than mining a concentrated one. See deuterium from seawater and the water cycle and fuel.

Treating the ocean as a fuel reservoir is apt precisely because using it does not diminish it in any perceptible way. The water returns, the hydrological cycle continues, and the deuterium ratio is maintained by nature. This is unlike a mineral deposit, which is depleted as it is worked; the ocean reservoir is effectively self-renewing on every timescale relevant to human energy use.

title: The Deuterium-To-Hydrogen Ratio
lede: The ratio of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen in ocean water is a precisely defined standard, which anchors any reasoning about the fuel supply.
body: The deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio of ocean water is codified as an international reference standard used across chemistry and Earth science. It corresponds to roughly 156 deuterium atoms per million hydrogen atoms. Because it is a defined, measured quantity, the fuel supply can be reasoned about with confidence rather than estimated loosely.

Having a defined ratio means the abundance of the fuel is not a matter of opinion or exploration luck. Any laboratory can verify the concentration, and the value is stable across the world ocean. Fuel-supply projections therefore rest on a measured physical constant, not on projected reserves.
Ratio is defined by an international water standard
About one deuterium atom per 6,400 hydrogen atoms
Value is stable and independently verifiable
Removes uncertainty from long-range fuel reasoning

This defined ratio underlies the claim that deuterium is effectively unlimited: a known concentration in a known reservoir gives a known, enormous inventory. See deuterium abundance and the ocean reservoir.
A constant you can build on

Basing a fuel-supply argument on a defined physical constant is far stronger than basing it on estimated reserves. Reserve figures are revised as exploration and technology change; the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio does not move. Any laboratory can confirm it, and it holds across the world ocean, so projections built on it inherit that stability rather than the uncertainty that clouds conventional reserve accounting.

title: What Bred Helium-3 Can Supply
lede: Helium-3 has uses with no easy substitute; a breeder that makes it in situ can supply those needs from a renewable source.
body: Helium-3 serves applications where alternatives are poor or absent. It enables ultra-low-temperature refrigeration that reaches the millikelvin range for quantum and superconducting systems, it is a preferred medium for neutron detection in security screening, and it supports certain forms of medical imaging. All of these have suffered from the scarcity of the isotope.

Because the legacy supply of helium-3 comes from decaying weapons tritium, these applications have competed for a shrinking inventory and faced recurring shortages. A breeder (Hyperion) producing about 1.97 kg/yr class of helium-3 as an operational byproduct offers a renewable supply that grows with the number of plants rather than depending on old stockpiles.
Millikelvin refrigeration for quantum and superconducting systems
Neutron detection for security and research
Supplied as a byproduct rather than drawn from a fixed inventory

The strategic value of helium-3 here is about physical scarcity and supply, not economics; no market or revenue claim is made. Yields are design targets, not measurements. See helium-3 bred in situ and a self-sustaining isotope supply.
Supply that grows with the fleet

The uses of helium-3 have long been throttled by how little of it exists, forcing researchers and hospitals to compete for a shrinking stock. A breeder that makes the isotope as a byproduct ties supply to how many machines run rather than to an aging inventory. As the fleet grows, so does the availability of an isotope that today is one of the scarcest useful materials on Earth.

title: Tritium Inventory And Decay
lede: Tritium's 12.3-year half-life means a working inventory must be managed actively, but it also guarantees no long-lived fuel legacy.
body: Tritium decays with a half-life of about 12.3 years. Roughly half of any inventory converts to helium-3 over that period. This has two consequences: the plant must breed and recover tritium continuously to maintain a working stock, and any tritium left behind at end of life decays away rather than persisting for millennia.

The same decay that requires active inventory management also means tritium is not a long-lived waste problem. What is not consumed becomes stable, valuable helium-3. There is no scenario in which a large tritium inventory lingers dangerously for geological time — physics removes it on a decadal scale.
Half-life about 12.3 years — decadal, not geological
Continuous breeding sustains the working inventory
Uncaptured tritium decays to useful helium-3
No long-lived fuel legacy at end of life
This decay behavior links the fuel cycle to the waste case. See tritium to helium-3 and self-sufficiency.

The 12.3-year half-life imposes a discipline and grants a reprieve at the same time. It requires continuous breeding and recovery to keep a working stock, so inventory management is a live operational task. But it also guarantees that nothing accumulates for the long term: within decades any tritium either is consumed, is recovered, or has decayed into stable helium-3, leaving no lingering fuel hazard.

title: Fuel Storage And Handling
lede: The stable fuel components are easy to store; tritium is handled with containment and accounting because it is radioactive and mobile.
body: Fusion fuel divides into stable and radioactive components. Deuterium and helium-3 are stable, non-radioactive, and stored like ordinary gases. Tritium is radioactive, chemically identical to hydrogen, and able to move into water and materials, so it is the component that governs storage design.

Tritium is kept in closed systems, often bound in metal hydrides that hold it safely, with multiple containment barriers and continuous accounting. Its low-energy beta emission cannot penetrate skin from outside, and its short half-life limits how long any release would persist. The working inventory at any moment is small.
Deuterium and helium-3 stored as ordinary stable gases
Tritium held in closed systems with layered containment
Small working inventory limits any consequence

Detailed safety barriers are covered in the safety-case pages; here the point is that the fuel itself is easy to store, with tritium the only component needing special care, and even that on a small scale. See fuel logistics and tritium inventory and decay.
The easy majority and the careful minority

Most of the fuel inventory — deuterium and helium-3 — is stable and stored without special measures, so storage design concentrates on the one radioactive component. Tritium is kept small in quantity, bound in metal hydrides, and wrapped in layered containment with continuous accounting. Because its emission is weak and its half-life short, even the careful minority of the inventory presents a modest, well-bounded task.

title: No Fissile Fuel In The Cycle
lede: Fusion fuel contains no uranium or plutonium, so the fuel cycle offers no pathway to weapons-usable fissile material.
body: The fuel is hydrogen and helium isotopes

The materials in the fusion fuel cycle are isotopes of hydrogen and helium, plus lithium for breeding. None of these is a fissile material. There is no uranium to enrich, no plutonium to separate, and no chain-reacting core. The proliferation concerns that surround fissile fuel simply do not apply to the fuel itself.

No uranium or plutonium anywhere in the fuel cycle
No enrichment of a fissile isotope
No weapons-usable material produced by fueling the plant
Fuel can be widely distributed without fissile safeguards
This concerns the fuel materials specifically. Tritium is handled responsibly for radiological reasons, addressed elsewhere. See compared to the uranium cycle and no fuel geopolitics.

A fuel cycle free of fissile material can be deployed broadly without the safeguards regime that fissile fuels demand, which is itself a supply advantage. There is no enrichment plant to inspect, no weapons-usable stream to track, and no diversion pathway to guard against. This makes the fuel compatible with wide, decentralized deployment rather than confined to tightly controlled sites.

title: The Water Cycle And Fuel
lede: Drawing deuterium from water does not consume water in any meaningful sense; the separated water returns to the hydrological cycle.
body: Separating deuterium takes in water, removes a minute fraction of its hydrogen atoms as the heavy isotope, and returns the rest. The water itself is not destroyed. Because deuterium is such a small fraction of the hydrogen present, the volume of water involved is tiny relative to any natural flow, and it rejoins the environment.

The amount touched to extract a plant's deuterium is negligible within that flow, and much of the fuel supply can draw on seawater rather than freshwater. The fuel supply does not compete meaningfully with drinking water or agriculture.
Water is returned after deuterium is separated
Only a minute fraction of hydrogen is removed
Seawater can be the source, sparing freshwater
The draw is negligible within the hydrological cycle

This page concerns water as a fuel source. The separate question of how little water a plant uses for cooling — very little, because direct energy conversion avoids a steam cycle — is covered in the water and resources pages. See the ocean reservoir and a sustainable fuel cycle.

Extracting deuterium borrows water briefly and returns nearly all of it, removing only a minute fraction of hydrogen atoms. Set against the immense flows of the hydrological cycle, the draw is imperceptible, and drawing on seawater spares freshwater entirely. The fuel supply therefore does not trade energy for water stress, a distinction that matters as water becomes a more contested resource.

title: The Fuel Supply Chain End To End
lede: From ocean water to fusion and back to bred fuel, the complete chain has few steps and no extractive bottleneck.
body: Seen end to end, the fusion fuel supply is short. Water is separated to yield deuterium. Deuterium and bred tritium fuse in the breeder (Hyperion). Neutrons breed fresh tritium in the lithium blanket, which is recovered and returned. Surplus tritium decays into helium-3, which can fuel the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) or serve other uses.

Unlike conventional chains, no step in this sequence depends on a mine, a well, or a region-specific deposit. The only external inputs are water and lithium, both abundant. Everything else is generated inside the plant. This is why the chain is resilient and why it scales without securing new resources.
Step 2: fuse deuterium with bred tritium
Step 3: breed and recover tritium in the blanket
Step 4: harvest helium-3 from decayed surplus tritium

The breeder makes the fuel; the burner uses the helium-3 it produces. Together they form a coherent supply picture rather than two isolated fuel demands. See the breeder-burner fuel link and the closed fuel cycle.

Laid out end to end, the fusion fuel chain is short and free of the chokepoints that define conventional supply: no mine, no well, no region-specific deposit, no refining monopoly. Its only external inputs are water and lithium, both abundant and dispersed, and its central steps happen inside the plant. Shortness and the absence of bottlenecks are what make the chain resilient.

title: Lithium Recycling In The Blanket
lede: Lithium in the breeding blanket is not destroyed by breeding tritium; it can be recovered and recycled, keeping the input demand small.
body: When blanket lithium absorbs a neutron and breeds tritium, the lithium atom is consumed in that specific reaction, but the surrounding lithium inventory remains and can be reprocessed. Blanket materials are managed so that lithium is recovered, re-enriched if needed, and returned to service rather than discarded after a single pass.

Re-enrichment can restore the desired isotope balance
Makeup demand stays small relative to lithium production
Lithium recycling turns the blanket into a largely closed material loop, consistent with the sustainability goals of the overall cycle. See lithium for breeding and blanket tritium recovery.

Because only the specific atoms that breed tritium are consumed, the bulk lithium inventory turns over slowly and can be recovered and re-enriched rather than discarded. That keeps the makeup demand small and turns the blanket into a nearly closed material loop. Recycling is what ensures the cycle's single mined input never grows into a significant extractive footprint over a plant's life.

title: Recovering Tritium From The Blanket
lede: Tritium bred in the lithium blanket must be extracted efficiently and returned to the plasma for the fuel cycle to close.
body: Breeding tritium is only half the task; the bred tritium must then be extracted from the blanket and fed back to the plasma. Recovery systems collect tritium from the blanket material and its coolant or purge stream, purify it, and route it to the fuel supply. High recovery efficiency is essential to maintaining self-sufficiency.

Every tritium atom that is bred but not recovered is a loss against the breeding ratio. A design may breed above unity locally yet fail to be self-sufficient if recovery and retention losses are high. This is why the program distinguishes local breeding from net delivered breeding and treats recovery as a first-order requirement.
Bred tritium is extracted from blanket material and purge streams
Recovered tritium is purified before returning to the plasma
Recovery losses count directly against the breeding ratio
Local breeding and net breeding are tracked separately
Demonstrating high-efficiency recovery at scale is open engineering; the breeder remains a design and simulation study. See tritium self-sufficiency and the breeding-ratio lever.
Recovery is where self-sufficiency is won or lost

Breeding tritium is necessary but not sufficient; the bred atoms must actually be extracted and returned, or they count for nothing. Recovery efficiency therefore sits at the heart of self-sufficiency, and it is the main reason local breeding can look better than net delivered breeding. A blanket that breeds well but recovers poorly can still fall short of closing the cycle.

Because helium-3 and helium-4 are chemically identical, they are separated by physical means that exploit their small mass difference, similar in spirit to how deuterium is separated from hydrogen. The quantities are small — a design-target class near 1.97 kg/yr per breeder — so the separation plant is correspondingly modest in scale.
Helium-3 collected from gases as tritium decays
Separated from helium-4 by mass-based physical methods
Purified to the level each application requires
Design-target output near a 1.97 kg/yr class per breeder

Purified helium-3 can fuel the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) or supply refrigeration, detection, and imaging uses. Yields are design targets, not measurements. See what bred helium-3 can supply and helium-3 bred in situ.

Because the annual helium-3 output is measured in a kilogram-scale class, the separation plant that isolates it from ordinary helium is modest, and it relies on the same mass-based physics used to separate other light isotopes. The task is one of purity and careful collection rather than throughput. The isotope emerges continuously as tritium decays, so recovery is a steady process rather than a batch event.

title: The Neutron Economy
lede: Every fusion neutron is a resource: it can breed tritium, multiply into more neutrons, or be lost, and balancing this budget sets the breeding ratio.
body: In a deuterium-tritium plant, the 14 MeV neutrons carry the energy and drive breeding. Each neutron can be captured in lithium to make tritium, multiplied into additional neutrons by certain materials, absorbed uselessly by structure, or leaked out. The tritium breeding ratio is the outcome of how this neutron budget is spent.

Designers raise the breeding ratio by adding neutron multipliers, enriching lithium-6 for reliable capture, retaining lithium-7 for its extra-neutron reaction, improving blanket coverage to reduce leakage, and choosing low-absorption structural materials. Each lever trades against engineering complexity and against the machine's other requirements.
Multipliers add neutrons to the budget
Low-absorption structures preserve neutrons for breeding
The neutron economy sets the achievable breeding ratio and also drives material activation, linking the fuel cycle to the waste case. See the breeding-ratio lever and lithium-6 versus lithium-7.

Each fusion neutron is spent only once, so the breeding ratio is ultimately an accounting of how carefully that budget is allocated. Multipliers add to the budget, enrichment directs it toward reliable capture, full coverage prevents leakage, and low-absorption structures avoid wasting it. Every lever trades against engineering complexity, which is why the neutron economy is one of the defining design problems of a breeding machine.

title: Breeding Ratio 1.1 — Near Self-Sufficiency
lede: A breeding ratio of 1.1 keeps a single machine fueled with a modest margin, prioritizing engineering simplicity over rapid fuel accumulation.
body: At a tritium breeding ratio of 1.1, the plant produces ten percent more tritium than it consumes. That margin covers recovery losses and sustains one machine's fuel supply, but it accumulates surplus slowly. It is the most conservative point in the breeder's design sweep and the least demanding on blanket engineering.

The advantage of a low breeding ratio is that it is easier to achieve: less aggressive multiplication, simpler blanket geometry, and more tolerance for losses. The cost is that there is little spare tritium to start additional machines quickly, so fleet growth from internally bred fuel is slow at this point.
Covers recovery losses for one machine
Slow accumulation of startup fuel for new plants
Even 1.1 net must be demonstrated in real blankets after recovery losses; local breeding can exceed net breeding. The breeder is a design and simulation study. See the 1.5 case and the 1.8 case.
The conservative anchor of the sweep

The 1.1 case anchors the conservative end of the design study, showing that self-sufficiency can be approached without aggressive neutron management. Its value is as a floor: if even this modest margin holds net of losses, the machine sustains itself. What it does not offer is rapid growth, because a ten-percent surplus builds startup fuel for new plants only slowly.

title: Breeding Ratio 1.5 — Comfortable Margin
lede: A breeding ratio of 1.5 gives a substantial fuel surplus, enough to absorb losses comfortably and to help start additional machines.
body: At a tritium breeding ratio of 1.5, the plant produces half again as much tritium as it burns. This surplus comfortably covers recovery and retention losses and leaves meaningful spare fuel. It is the middle point of the breeder's design sweep, balancing achievability against the ability to grow a fleet.

Why the middle point is attractive

A 1.5 ratio is demanding enough to require good neutron management — multipliers, lithium enrichment, and full blanket coverage — but not so aggressive that it dominates the design. The surplus it generates can provide the initial tritium charge for a next machine on a reasonable timescale, or accumulate as helium-3.
Comfortably absorbs recovery and retention losses
Provides startup fuel for additional plants
The 1.5 value is a design-sweep point, not a demonstrated blanket result; net breeding after losses is the figure that matters. See the 1.1 case and the 1.8 case.

The 1.5 case is attractive because it asks for competent but not extreme neutron management while still generating enough surplus to seed additional machines on a sensible timescale. It sits where the trade between engineering difficulty and fleet-growth potential is most balanced. For that reason it often serves as the reference point when reasoning about how a fleet could bootstrap itself from internally bred fuel.

title: Breeding Ratio 1.8 — Strong Margin
lede: A breeding ratio of 1.8 maximizes fuel surplus and fleet-growth potential, at the cost of the most demanding blanket engineering.
body: At a tritium breeding ratio of 1.8, the plant produces nearly twice the tritium it consumes. This is the most aggressive point in the breeder's design sweep. It builds a large surplus quickly, enabling faster fleet growth and generous helium-3 production, but it requires the most capable neutron management.

The engineering cost of a high ratio

Reaching 1.8 net demands effective neutron multiplication, high blanket coverage, well-chosen lithium enrichment, and low structural absorption — all working together with minimal recovery losses. It is the point most sensitive to the gap between local breeding and net delivered breeding, and therefore the one requiring the strongest engineering evidence.
Roughly eighty percent margin over consumption
Fastest accumulation of startup fuel and helium-3
Most demanding on multipliers, coverage, and recovery
Most sensitive to the local-versus-net breeding distinction

The program explicitly flags reconciling a 1.8 breeding ratio between local and net accounting as open work; this is a design target, not a measured result. See the 1.5 case and the breeding-ratio lever.

The 1.8 case marks the aggressive end of the sweep, where surplus accumulates fastest but every element of neutron management must perform near its best simultaneously. It is also the value most exposed to the gap between local and net breeding, since high losses erode a high local ratio quickly. The program flags reconciling 1.8 between local and net accounting as explicit open work.

title: The Breeder-Burner Fuel Link
lede: The breeder (Hyperion) makes helium-3; the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) uses it — two machines joined by a shared fuel product.
body: The two Kronos machines are connected through helium-3. The breeder (Hyperion) produces helium-3 in situ as a byproduct of its deuterium-tritium operation. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) fuses deuterium with helium-3. The output of one machine is a fuel for the other, which is why the fuel picture is best understood as a system rather than two separate demands.

A deuterium-helium-3 machine on its own faces a fuel problem, because terrestrial helium-3 is scarce. Pairing it with a breeder that makes helium-3 turns that scarcity into a solvable supply question. The breeder's byproduct becomes the burner's feedstock, and both draw their other input, deuterium, from water.
Breeder helium-3 output is a burner fuel input
The pairing addresses the burner's helium-3 scarcity problem
Longer-term lunar helium-3 can supplement the breeder route

Both machines are design and simulation studies; the burner's commercial fuel supply is gated on scaling helium-3, and no net-power claim is made for either. See the Earth-Moon fuel picture and the deuterium-helium-3 cycle.
A system, not two fuel problems

Viewed separately, the burner has a helium-3 scarcity problem and the breeder has a helium-3 surplus; viewed together, one solves the other. Treating the two machines as a single fuel system is the honest framing, because the breeder's byproduct is exactly the burner's feedstock and both share deuterium from water. The link is what makes a deuterium-helium-3 machine practical on Earth at all.

title: The Earth-Moon Fuel Picture
lede: Helium-3 can come from breeding on Earth and, over the longer term, from lunar sources — an honest look at both routes.
body: There are two credible routes to helium-3 for the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). The near-term, on-Earth route is breeding it in the breeder (Hyperion), where it emerges as an operational byproduct. The longer-term route is lunar helium-3, deposited in the Moon's surface by the solar wind over billions of years, which would require an off-world extraction and transport program.

The breeder route is available first because it depends only on running the machine. The lunar route is a larger, later possibility that would supplement rather than precede it. Presenting these honestly means treating breeding as the primary near-term source and lunar helium-3 as a strategic long-horizon supplement, not a prerequisite.
On-Earth breeding is the near-term helium-3 source
Lunar helium-3 is a longer-horizon supplement
The lunar route requires substantial off-world infrastructure
Neither route requires terrestrial mining of helium-3

Lunar helium-3 is a future capability, not a current supply; the burner's fuel plan does not depend on it existing yet. Both machines remain design and simulation studies. See the breeder-burner link and helium-3 scarcity.

Honesty about helium-3 means being clear about sequence: breeding on Earth is available first because it needs only a running machine, while lunar helium-3 is a larger, later supplement that would require substantial off-world infrastructure. Presenting the lunar route as a long-horizon addition, not a prerequisite, keeps the near-term fuel plan grounded in what the breeder can actually produce.

title: A Self-Sustaining Isotope Supply
lede: Running the breeder generates a renewable stream of tritium, helium-3, and neutrons — isotope products that sustain themselves from abundant inputs.
body: Operating the breeder (Hyperion) turns abundant inputs into a stream of otherwise scarce isotopes. From water-derived deuterium and lithium, the machine produces a roughly 4 kg/yr class of tritium, a helium-3 class near 1.97 kg/yr, and a flux of 14 MeV neutrons. These are renewable in the sense that they regenerate as long as the plant runs.

All output figures are computed design targets for a machine entering construction in Q2 2027, not measured yields, and no economic value is claimed. See what bred helium-3 can supply and the closed fuel cycle.

The isotope stream is self-sustaining because each product feeds the next stage: tritium fuels the plant and seeds new machines, its surplus decays to helium-3, helium-3 fuels the burner, and the neutrons breed the next tritium. Nothing in this loop depends on depleting a finite deposit; it runs on water and lithium, so the isotopes it yields are renewable in the only sense that matters for supply.

title: Fusion Fuel Versus Fission And Fossil
lede: A side-by-side look at where each fuel comes from, how long it lasts, and what it leaves behind — comparing fuel cycles only.
body: Comparing fuel cycles clarifies why fusion's fuel case differs so sharply from conventional energy. Fossil fuel is mined or drilled, region-concentrated, and burned into the atmosphere. Fissile fuel is mined and enriched, leaving long-lived spent fuel. Fusion fuel is separated from water and bred on site, with no long-lived fuel legacy.

Fusion fuel is universal, not region-concentrated
Its supply horizon is geological, not decadal
It leaves no long-lived spent fuel and emits no combustion products
Material activation and plant waste are covered in the low-neutron and waste pages; here the subject is fuel. See versus the uranium cycle and versus fossil supply chains.
A consistent pattern across the row

What stands out in the comparison is not any single cell but the consistency of the pattern: on source, distribution, longevity, and legacy, the fusion fuel cycle is the more favorable entry on every line. That consistency is why the fuel case is treated as a genuine differentiator, while being careful to note that this is a fuel-cycle comparison, not a full plant lifecycle or any economic ranking.

title: Fuel Reserves Versus Global Demand
lede: Setting the deuterium reservoir against global energy demand shows why the supply is described as effectively unlimited.
body: Global energy demand, though large, is finite and measurable. The deuterium inventory of the ocean, multiplied by the energy density of fusion, is so much larger that the two quantities live on different scales entirely. Dividing the reservoir by demand yields a supply horizon measured in geological time.

Why 'effectively unlimited' is the honest phrase

Nothing physical is truly infinite, so the careful phrasing is 'effectively unlimited': the reservoir is finite but so vast, relative to demand, that depletion is not a meaningful concern on any human or civilizational timescale. Even large growth in demand does not change this conclusion, because the gap in scale is so wide.
Reservoir dwarfs demand by many orders of magnitude
Supply horizon is geological, not economic
Robust even under aggressive demand growth
This compares energy content of the fuel reservoir to energy demand; it makes no economic claim about supply. See longevity of supply and energy density.

The care taken with the phrase effectively unlimited is deliberate. Nothing physical is truly infinite, so the claim is stated as a comparison of scales: the reservoir exceeds demand by so many orders of magnitude that depletion is not a meaningful concern on any timescale a civilization would plan around. Stating it precisely is stronger than overclaiming, and it survives even aggressive assumptions about future demand growth.

title: The Closed Fuel Cycle
lede: A closed fuel cycle regenerates its own fuel internally, so the plant depends on abundant external inputs only, not on a continuing fuel supply.
body: A fuel cycle is closed when the plant makes as much fuel as it uses, so that after startup it does not draw down an external fuel store. The breeder (Hyperion) is designed to close its tritium cycle by breeding tritium in the blanket and recovering it, taking in only deuterium from water and lithium for breeding.

A closed cycle breaks that dependence: once running, the plant sustains itself from abundant, universally available inputs. Closure is what converts fuel abundance into genuine fuel independence.

Only deuterium and lithium enter from outside
No continuing external fuel stream is required

Closure is a design objective for machines still in simulation; net breeding after recovery losses must be demonstrated, and the program tracks the local-versus-net gap. Construction begins Q2 2027. See self-sufficiency and a sustainable fuel cycle.

Abundant inputs alone do not free a plant from external suppliers; closing the loop does. A closed cycle regenerates its fuel internally so that, after startup, it draws only on water and lithium. This is the step that turns fuel abundance into fuel independence, and it is why closure — demonstrated net of recovery losses — is treated as a first-order design objective rather than a nicety.

title: Fuel Purity Requirements
lede: Fusion plasmas are sensitive to impurities, so fuel must be prepared and kept clean — a handling requirement, not a supply constraint.
body: Why purity matters to the plasma

A fusion plasma performs best when the fuel is clean. Heavier impurity atoms radiate energy away and dilute the reacting ions, degrading performance. Deuterium, tritium, and helium-3 must therefore be prepared to high purity and kept free of contamination as they cycle through the plant.
