A handling task, not a scarcity

Purity is a processing requirement, not a limit on how much fuel exists. The isotopes are abundant or bred; the work is in cleaning and maintaining them. Recovered fuel — unburned deuterium, tritium, and helium products — is reprocessed and returned to the required purity rather than discarded, keeping the cycle efficient.
Impurities radiate energy and dilute the fuel
Fuel isotopes are purified before entering the plasma
Recovered fuel is cleaned and recycled, not wasted
Purity is about processing, not fuel availability
Reprocessing recovered fuel to purity is part of what makes the closed cycle efficient, and it applies to both machines. See the closed fuel cycle and storage and handling.

Purity is sometimes mistaken for a supply limit, but it is a processing requirement that the closed cycle already accommodates. Fuel is cleaned before it enters the plasma and recovered fuel is recleaned rather than discarded, so purity work supports efficiency rather than constraining availability. The isotopes remain abundant or bred; keeping them clean is ordinary, well-bounded chemistry.

title: Fuel-Cycle Sustainability Metrics
lede: A short set of physical measures captures why the fusion fuel cycle is sustainable: input abundance, loop closure, and waste class.
body: Sustainability can be made concrete with a few physical measures rather than slogans. For a fuel cycle the relevant ones are: how abundant the inputs are, how completely the loop closes, how small the fuel mass is per unit energy, and what class of waste the fuel leaves behind. The fusion cycle scores well on each.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 260" width="100%" style="max-width:680px;height:auto;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="1" y="1" width="678" height="258" rx="10" fill="#232C39" stroke="#B8933F" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="15" fill="#D4AD5C" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">Fuel-cycle inputs, by origin</text><rect x="60" y="62.0" width="90" height="119.0" fill="#D4AD5C" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="166" y="125.5" font-size="12" fill="#D4AD5C" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">Bred / recovered internally</text><rect x="60" y="181.0" width="90" height="51.0" fill="#3a4757" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="166" y="210.5" font-size="12" fill="#E8ECF1" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">Abundant external (water + lithium)</text><rect x="60" y="62" width="90" height="170" fill="none" stroke="#B8933F" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

No single measure makes a cycle sustainable; the combination does. Abundant inputs guarantee longevity, closure guarantees independence, tiny fuel mass guarantees light logistics, and the absence of long-lived fuel waste and fissile material guarantees a clean and safe legacy. Together they describe a fuel cycle built to run indefinitely.
Abundance gives a geological supply horizon
Closure gives independence from external fuel
Small fuel mass gives simple, secure logistics
Clean waste class gives a light long-term legacy
Closure and breeding figures are design targets for machines still in simulation, not demonstrated results. No metric here is economic. See a sustainable fuel cycle and the glossary.
Why the combination is the point

No one metric carries the sustainability claim; it is the combination that does. Abundant inputs give longevity, closure gives independence, small fuel mass gives light logistics, and a clean waste class gives a light legacy — each checkable, and together describing a cycle built to run indefinitely. Reading them as a set, rather than cherry-picking one, is what makes the assessment honest.

title: Fuel And Sustainability Glossary
lede: Definitions of the key fuel-cycle and sustainability terms used across these pages, stated plainly and honestly.
body: Deuterium — stable heavy hydrogen isotope (one proton, one neutron); the primary fusion fuel, separated from water.
Tritium — radioactive hydrogen isotope (one proton, two neutrons); half-life about 12.3 years; bred in the lithium blanket.
Helium-3 — stable, scarce helium isotope; produced when tritium decays; fuels the burner and serves refrigeration, detection, and imaging.
Lithium — abundant element used in the breeding blanket; captures neutrons to make tritium.
Tritium breeding ratio (TBR) — tritium atoms produced per tritium atom consumed; studied at 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8.
Neutron economy — how fusion neutrons are allocated among breeding, multiplication, absorption, and leakage.
Closed fuel cycle — a cycle that regenerates its fuel internally, needing only abundant external inputs.
Local vs net breeding — breeding measured before losses versus the fuel actually delivered after recovery losses.

How to read these terms together

These terms interlock: deuterium and lithium enter, neutrons breed tritium, tritium sustains the plant and decays to helium-3, and the loop closes. Read as a sequence rather than isolated definitions, they describe a single self-sustaining fuel cycle. Every quantity attached to them on these pages is a computed design target for machines still in simulation, never a measurement or an economic figure.
